title: Affordable housing refinancing exemption for Victoria Park Community Homes
subtitle: Public health dental program update, infection prevention and safe water inspections, and a homeless shelter petition received.
overview: The Community and Health Services Committee recommended that Victoria Park Community Homes receive an exemption from the Region's Affordable Housing Refinancing Policy {{vote:m1}}. The not-for-profit provider was awarded a forgivable loan from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for repairs and retrofit of one Cambridge property. The loan would push the property's total encumbrance above the policy's 90 percent limit. The exemption is intended to let the repairs go ahead and improve conditions for tenants. Staff also plan a fuller review of the 90 percent threshold.

The committee received two Public Health reports for information. The dental program update said the federal Canadian Dental Care Plan has expanded coverage but that co-payments, delays and reduced acceptance of Healthy Smiles Ontario still leave some vulnerable residents with the Public Health Dental Clinic as their only option. The inspection report described growing demand for infection prevention and control, drinking water and recreational water inspections.
The committee also received a petition to support homeless shelters for information. Its recommendation on the exemption goes to Council for adoption. The next meeting is September 8, 2026.

decisions.item: Victoria Park Community Homes refinancing exemption
decisions.detail: The committee recommended exempting one Cambridge property owned by Victoria Park Community Homes from the 90 percent encumbrance limit in the Refinancing of Affordable Housing Projects policy, and authorizing the Commissioner of Community Services and Chief Financial Officer to sign the related agreements in a form satisfactory to the Regional Solicitor {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Staff said the exemption is low risk: the provider is in good standing financially and operationally, about half of the property's current encumbrance is already forgivable loans, and CMHC's own policy allows up to 120 percent.
One councillor asked where the Region ranks if the property were defaulted or sold. Staff said the Region sits second, behind the federal government, after postponement agreements.

Councillors supported the exemption but wanted it to stay a one-off. They backed the planned policy review, noting the context the policy operates in has changed and the 90 percent threshold may need updating.

One councillor asked whether the provider could stop offering affordable housing after the 10-year loan term. Staff said other funding agreements and the provider's not-for-profit mandate would keep it affordable, and that a private owner would be a different case.
On the Public Health reports, councillors said prevention work often goes unrecognized because success means no outbreaks, and one wished the cost savings could be quantified.
